e.etymology: A modern American blend of Jasmine and the -lynn ending, one of several spellings of Jazlyn that spread in the 2000s. It has no meaning apart from its parts; jasmine is the fragrant flower.
A short form of Emily, Emilia and Emma, and a spelling of Emmy. It is also used as a form of Amy, from Old French Amee, beloved.

assoc.t: sounds like the Emmy, television's top award

e.etymology: A compound of Bella, Italian for beautiful and a short form of Isabella, and Rose, the flower. Written as one word it is a recent American creation.
A respelling of Kensley, a modern surname-style name close to Kinsley and Kenzie, finished with the -leigh spelling of the English word for a meadow or clearing.
A modern American coinage that puts a Z on the sound of Kayleigh, Hayley and Bailey. It has no meaning of its own.
A modern Indian compound of Sanskrit veda, sacred knowledge and the name of the oldest Hindu scriptures, and ansh, a part or portion.
A modern American coinage that joins the Ez- sound of Ezra and Esme with the -lyn ending of Evelyn and Adalyn. It has no meaning of its own.
A recent coinage that puts a fashionable X on the sound of Zamira and Samira. Samira is an Arabic name for a companion in evening conversation.
In Polish and Slovak, Karol is the men's name Charles, from Latin Carolus and Germanic karl, free man. In the US it is mostly a girls' name in Spanish-speaking families, a K spelling of Carol.

assoc.t: Karol G, Colombian reggaeton star

e.etymology: A spelling of Anaya, a name that rose in the US in the 2000s alongside Amaya, Aniyah and Janiya. Anaya is also a Spanish surname.
From Hebrew atarah, crown. In the Bible, Atarah is a wife of Jerahmeel in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles; the modern Hebrew form is Atara.
A spelling of Amaya or Amaia finished with the -iah of Biblical names. Amaia is a Basque name, from amaia, the end, made known by the 1879 Spanish novel Amaya.
The English word for a shaded garden shelter of trees or vines, its spelling shaped by Latin arbor, tree. As a first name it is new, part of the wave of nature names like Aspen and Linden.

assoc.t: Arbor Day, the tree-planting holiday
Ann Arbor, Michigan college town
Arbor snowboards and skateboards

e.etymology: From Greek astron, star, familiar as the astro- in astronaut and astronomy. Its use as a first name is recent.

assoc.t: Astro, the family dog on The Jetsons
Astro Boy, Japanese manga and anime robot hero
Houston Astros baseball team
Astro gaming headsets
Amazon Astro home robot

e.note: Best known as the Jetsons' dog and as Astro Boy, so some will hear a cartoon or pet name.

e.etymology: A Spanish blend of Maria and Celia, also spelled Marisela. It was most popular in the US in the 1970s in Mexican American families.
A modern elaboration of Audrey with the -anna ending of Brianna and Adrianna. Audrey comes from the Old English name Aethelthryth, noble strength.
A spelling of Winona, from Dakota winuna, firstborn daughter. The Dakota used it as a birth-order title; English speakers adopted it as a given name in the 1800s.

assoc.t: Wynonna Judd, country singer, by sound
actress Winona Ryder, by sound

e.etymology: A modern blend of Jess, from Jessica, and the -lyn ending of Jocelyn and Kaitlyn; a shorter form of Jessalyn. It has no meaning apart from its parts.
A double-L spelling of Elena, the Italian and Spanish form of Helen, also read as Ellen with an added -a. Helen is Greek Helene, traditionally linked to words for torch or bright light.
An English and French surname from medieval pet forms of Matthew (Masse, Mace). As a first name it also draws on the word mace, the medieval war club, and is used as a short form of Mason.

assoc.t: Mace pepper spray
Mace Windu, Jedi master in Star Wars
mace, a spiked medieval war club
mace, the spice made from the nutmeg seed coat

e.note: Mace is a pepper spray brand and a medieval club; some people will think of those first.

e.etymology: A Hebrew name from tal, dew, with the ending -i, my. It is also used as a short form of Talia.

assoc.t: Tali'Zorah, crew member in the Mass Effect games

e.etymology: A respelling of Mason, the English occupational surname for a stoneworker, from Old French masson. This spelling is given to girls more often than boys.
A respelling of Bristol, the English port city, whose name is Old English brycg, bridge, and stow, place. Bristol took off as a US girls' name after 2008 with Bristol Palin.

assoc.t: Bristol, port city in southwest England, by sound
Bristol Motor Speedway, NASCAR track, by sound

e.meaning: ruling goddess; a name of Durga
e.etymology: From Sanskrit Ishani, the feminine of Ishana, ruler or lord, a name of Shiva. Ishani is a name of his consort, the goddess Parvati or Durga.
A double-M spelling of Emery, from medieval Germanic names: Amalric, joining amal, vigor, and ric, ruler, or else a form of Henry, home ruler. It reached modern use by way of the English surname.

assoc.t: emery, the abrasive in emery boards, by sound

e.etymology: The English adverb truly, from Old English treowlice, faithfully. Its best-known earlier bearer is Truly Scrumptious in the 1968 film Chitty Chitty Bang Bang.

assoc.t: Truly Hard Seltzer
Truly Scrumptious in Chitty Chitty Bang Bang

e.note: Truly is one of the best-selling hard seltzer brands in the US.

e.etymology: The word love, or lovely, finished with the -lyn ending of Evelyn and Jocelyn. It has no meaning beyond its parts.
A 20th-century respelling of Nicky, the pet form of Nicole, Nicola and Nicholas. All come from Greek Nikolaos: nike, victory, and laos, people.
namesakes: Nikki Haley (former governor and UN ambassador)

assoc.t: Darling Nikki, Prince song from Purple Rain

e.etymology: A 20th-century American coinage derived from twilight, first spelled Twila. Choreographer Twyla Tharp made the y spelling familiar.
namesakes: Twyla Sands (cafe waitress on Schitt's Creek)

e.etymology: From a surname taken from places called Kelton in northern England and Scotland; the -ton is Old English tun, a farm or settlement. It joined Colton and Dalton as a first name in the late 1900s.
An English spelling of Yvette, shaped by the look of Eve. Yvette is the French feminine pet form of Yves, from a Germanic word for the yew tree.
A 2000s American name in the family of Aniyah, Janiyah and Saniyah, built on the sound of Tanya or Tania with the -iyah ending. Tanya is the Russian short form of Tatiana.
